Return Of Part V: Rules and Systems

Chapter 14 Preliminary draft

Rules of the Road

Taxes, wash sales, settlement and accredited status.

Rules about taxes, settlement and day trading change the real cost of every trade, so learn them before you place one, and write them into your own policy.

These are study notes as of November 19, 2026. They cover US rules only. Rules change, brokers apply them in different ways, and your own situation may differ. A tax professional is the authority on your taxes.

Day trading and margin

For years, a margin account that made four or more day trades in five business days was flagged as a pattern day trader and had to hold $25,000 in equity. FINRA replaced that. Its Regulatory Notice 26-10 says new intraday margin standards replace the day trading margin requirements in their entirety, including the day trade count and the $25,000 minimum. The effective date is June 4, 2026. Firms that need more time may phase the change in until October 20, 2027, so check what your own broker does today.

The speed bump is gone, but the risk is not. The new standard asks whether your account has enough equity to cover your exposure during the day, and a customer who repeatedly fails to cover an intraday deficit can face a 90-day trading restriction. Your own daily trade cap now does the job the old rule did by accident.

Settlement and cash accounts

US stock trades settle one business day after the trade (T+1). The SEC shortened the standard cycle from T+2 to T+1, with a compliance date of May 28, 2024, as its press release on the rule states. FINRA’s guide to cash accounts explains the practical effect: you must pay for a buy by the settlement date, and a firm can restrict an account that does not. Brokers commonly call it a good faith violation when you buy with cash from a sale that has not settled, then sell the new position before that earlier sale settles. In a cash account, trade with settled money.

Taxes

The IRS says a gain or loss on an asset held for more than one year is long-term. Held one year or less, it is short-term, and net short-term gains are taxed as ordinary income.

The same page says that if capital losses exceed gains, you can deduct up to $3,000 against other income ($1,500 if married filing separately), and you can carry the rest forward to later years.

Wash sales

IRS Publication 550 describes a wash sale: you sell stock at a loss and, within 30 days before or after the sale, buy substantially identical stock. It lists buying that stock for your IRA or Roth IRA as a trigger. Revenue Ruling 2008-5 adds that the loss is disallowed in that case and the IRA’s basis does not go up.

Your broker does not see your whole picture. The Form 1099-B instructions require a broker to report a disallowed loss when the sale and purchase are in the same account and have the same CUSIP number. Reporting across accounts is permitted but not required. A loss you cannot deduct is still your responsibility, even when no form shows it. Track wash sales in the journal.

Index options

Publication 550 says nonequity options, a group that includes broad-based stock index options, fall under the 60/40 rule: 60% of the gain or loss is long-term and 40% is short-term, however long you held. SPX is a broad-based index option. An option on an ETF such as SPY is an option on shares of a fund, not on an index, so it is generally taxed under the ordinary rules. The IRS pages above do not name SPY, so confirm this with a tax professional.

Accredited investor status

Many private offerings are open only to accredited investors, who qualify by income, net worth or certain credentials. On September 30, 2026, the SEC opened public comment on new ways to qualify, including passing an exam that FINRA would develop. It is a proposal, not a rule. Nothing changes for you until the SEC acts. Private offerings sit outside this method for now.

Your own trade cap now does the job the old rule did by accident.

Open questions

  • What daily trade cap replaces the old day trading limit, and how will the journal enforce it?
  • Where will you log wash sale windows so that a purchase in any account, IRA included, is caught?
  • Will you trade in a cash account, a margin account, or both, and what settled-funds rule goes in the policy?
  • Which tax professional will review the policy each year?
  • Do you want index options in the plan at all, and at which Ladder level?
